---
title: "Week 4 · Cause and effect in the RCT. Hypothesis testing. t-tests"
subtitle: "Null and alternative hypotheses, the two error types and the p-value, applied to two field experiments"
---

The week turns the causal language of Week 3 into a testable procedure. It
introduces hypothesis testing in the Neyman-Pearson framework and then works
through two randomised experiments, a school deworming programme in Kenya and a
conditional cash transfer, to see how checks-and-balances tables and t-tests
are used to read an RCT.

## Slides

The 2024/25 deck is titled *Cause and Effect in the RCT. Hypothesis testing.
T-tests. Examples. Central Limit Theorem.* The 2023/24 PDF was shared as *Week
04. Cause and Effect in the RCT. Hypothesis testing. T-tests* and is longer
(78 pages against 60); the Central Limit Theorem is not in its title.

## What the deck covers

-   **Hypothesis testing**: the Neyman-Pearson approach, the steps of a test,
    the two errors a test can make, the p-value and the level of significance;
    examples on stunting and education and on raven colour; homework.
-   **Examples of hypothesis testing** from a nutrition education RCT:
    research design, checks and balances, balance of household size, and how
    to identify whether the intervention helped.
-   **Effects of a deworming pill**: the Primary School Deworming Project
    timeline, checks and balances between groups, immediate effects on health
    and school participation, long-term economic effects, and costs and
    benefits.
-   **t-tests with conditional cash transfers**: cause and effect, what makes
    the difference in enrolment rates a causal effect, good controls in an RCT,
    checking that ceteris paribus holds, the checks-and-balances table, the
    t-test algorithm with worked examples, and conclusions.
-   Homework, readings (Chapters 1 and 2 of *Mastering 'Metrics*) and the key
    concepts checklist: causal meaning of averages, random sample variation,
    type I and type II errors, significance level, p-value, and the standard
    error of a sample mean.

## Data used

The examples in this week are read from the published tables of the studies
discussed; the images are in
